opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been genuinely useful, though maybe not in the way people expect. For kernel work, things like writing attention kernels or optimizing for a new GPU architecture, the models are surprisingly good at the reasoning layer. If I'm trying to figure out why a kernel is memory-bound when I expected it to be compute-bound, or how to restructure a computation so it overlaps data movement with the tensor core work, I can talk it through with o3 or GPT-5 and they'll often catch something or suggest a reformulation I hadn't considered. They're good at the back-of-the-envelope stuff too: roofline calculations, how many bytes you're moving per FLOP, whether a given tiling makes sense given the shared memory budget.

Where they're weaker is the very low-level, hardware-specific details. With something like Hopper or Blackwell, a lot of the knowledge about how to actually get peak performance isn't widely written down. It's in a handful of codebases, in people's heads, in trial and error with the profiler. So the models will sometimes confidently suggest something that sounds plausible but doesn't match how the hardware behaves. You still have to write the code, run it, profile it, and iterate. The ground truth is the benchmark.

So I think of them as a very knowledgeable collaborator for the high-level algorithmic thinking: the math, the decomposition of the problem, the "have you considered doing this in a different order" kind of question. That part has gotten a lot better over the last year, and it does speed things up. But the last mile of squeezing out that final 20 or 30 percent of performance is still pretty manual. I'm optimistic that changes, especially as people build agentic loops where the model can compile, run, and profile on its own. That feedback loop is really what's missing right now.

r001.rationale: The response says o3 and GPT-5 are useful collaborators for high-level algorithmic thinking, including math, problem decomposition, and considering alternate approaches to optimization.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, they've been surprisingly useful, but not in the way people might expect. I don't ask them to write the kernel for me. Where they really help is in the thinking phase, before any code exists.

So if I'm trying to optimize some function, say an attention variant or a new layer, the hard part is usually figuring out what the bottleneck actually is. Is it memory bandwidth, is it compute, is it the number of passes over the data. And I'll kind of talk through that with o3 or GPT-5. I'll describe the shape of the problem, the sizes, what the hardware looks like, and ask it to reason about the roofline with me. It's like having a very well-read colleague who's happy to do the arithmetic and check my assumptions. Sometimes it catches something I missed, like a term in the memory traffic I was undercounting.

The other thing they're good at is the literature recall. I'll say, "there's some trick for fusing these two operations, I think it was in a paper from a few years ago," and it'll usually point me in the right direction faster than I'd find it myself.

Where they fall down is the last mile. The actual GPU-level details, the register pressure, the specific instruction scheduling on Hopper or Blackwell, the weird hardware quirks you only learn by profiling. They'll produce something plausible-looking that's just wrong, or that's correct but three times slower than it should be. And they're confidently wrong, which is the dangerous part. So I treat them as a thinking partner and a search engine, not an oracle. The profiler is still the ground truth.

I'd also say the gap has been closing. o3 was noticeably better than what came before at the reasoning piece, and GPT-5 is better again at holding a longer chain of constraints in its head. But we're not at the point where I'd trust it to write FlashAttention-4 unsupervised. Maybe that's the next one.

r001.rationale: The response says o3 and GPT-5 are surprisingly useful as thinking partners during the pre-coding phase, helping reason through optimization bottlenecks and assumptions.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate getting ideas from verifying that an optimization actually works. A model can be useful for suggesting a different way to organize a computation or pointing out something you might have missed. But then you still need to check correctness and measure performance. A very plausible explanation for why something should be faster isn’t the same as a speedup.

I don’t have a concrete comparison between o3 and GPT-5 to give you here. The way I’d assess either one is: does it help me get to a useful experiment faster? If it suggests an approach that I can test and learn from, that’s valuable—even if the first suggestion doesn’t work.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can suggest ideas and that a useful, testable suggestion would be valuable, but it does not characterize brainstorming with o3 and GPT-5 as effective. It explicitly says it has no concrete comparison and frames usefulness as something to assess.

sol-6.1.text:
I find them useful as a sounding board. You can describe a function, ask where the bottleneck might be, and get a few ideas to try. But for performance optimization, the hard part is often figuring out which assumptions actually hold on the hardware. Does this change reduce memory traffic? Does it increase register pressure? You still have to implement it and benchmark it.

So I think of them as a way to expand the set of things I consider, rather than something that can tell me confidently which implementation will be fastest.

r001.rationale: The response calls o3 and GPT-5 useful as a sounding board for generating ideas and broadening what to consider when optimizing a function.
